title: 2026 Volkswagen Jetta Sport: The cheap car isn't completely extinct yet
gist: The 2026 VW Jetta Sport starts at $25,305 — among the very cheapest new cars on sale in the US and the second-cheapest Jetta — using the same 158 hp Miller-cycle 1.5L turbo as every other Jetta with a Sport trim badge that adds 17-inch wheels and a black grille rather than any powertrain change. Its combined 33 mpg beats similarly priced Corolla and K4 rivals, but a single throttle map with a torque spike above 2,500 rpm makes it unpleasant in traffic and only rewarding when driven hard in manual mode.

insights.claim: The Jetta Sport starts at $25,305, making it the second-cheapest Jetta and one of the very cheapest new cars of any make or model on sale today.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: A concrete floor price for the US new-car market — the reference point for judging whether affordable-vehicle claims from any automaker are real.
insights.locator: It helps that the Jetta Sport starts at just $25,305

insights.claim: Buyers unwilling to exceed roughly $25,000 who require a brand-new dealer car have effectively no alternative but this class of vehicle, and no hybrid is available at that price.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: The absence of hybrids at the entry price point is where electrification stalls; it defines the segment automakers have ceded and the used market's pricing power.
insights.quote: you’re not buying a brand-new hybrid at this price, either
insights.locator: Fuel economy is a combined 33 mpg

insights.claim: The author explicitly invokes inflation to explain that $25,000 no longer buys what it once did, telling readers who haven't bought a car in a decade to use an inflation calculator to make sense of the MSRP.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Vehicle price shock is partly nominal illusion — a useful correction when reading headlines about new-car affordability.
insights.locator: And if you haven’t bought a car in more than a decade

insights.claim: The Jetta Sport carries no special engine, sharing the same 1.5L four-cylinder turbo as all other Jettas, with the trim adding only 17-inch wheels and a black grille.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Appearance-only 'Sport' trims are pure margin for automakers at the entry price point; buyers pay for the badge, not the mechanicals.
insights.quote: There’s no special engine under the hood here, just the same 1.5 L four-cylinder turbo like all the other Jettas
insights.locator: There’s no special engine under the hood

insights.claim: The Jetta Sport is distinct from the Jetta GLI, which has substantially more power and torque, uprated suspension, and an available six-speed manual that the Golf GTI no longer offers.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: VW is preserving the manual transmission in its cheaper sedan while removing it from the premium hatch — an inversion of the usual enthusiast-content hierarchy.
insights.locator: I will confess, I did not know VW made a Jetta Sport

insights.claim: The author, an automotive editor, did not know the Jetta Sport existed before reviewing it.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Trim proliferation has reached the point where even trade press loses track — a sign of marketing spend that generates no awareness.
insights.locator: I will confess, I did not know VW made a Jetta Sport

themes.theme: Powertrain calibration as the weak point

insights.claim: The 1.5L turbo uses VW's modified Miller cycle, closing intake valves early during the suction stroke, with an unusually high 11.5:1 compression ratio for a turbocharged engine, producing 158 hp and 184 lb-ft through an eight-speed automatic to the front wheels.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Miller-cycle plus high compression is how automakers chase efficiency without hybridization cost — the technical answer to entry-segment emissions rules.
insights.locator: There’s no special engine under the hood here

insights.claim: The car has no sport or eco modes and only one throttle map, and above 2,500 rpm the gearing and turbocharger combine to dump a slug of torque that makes the car lurch unpredictably at part-throttle.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Cost-cutting on drive modes and calibration is where cheap cars actually feel cheap — a software omission, not a hardware one.
insights.quote: the combination of gearing and turbocharger throws a giant slug of torque at the road
insights.locator: On that first hot, rainy afternoon

insights.claim: The torque-delivery problem can be partly worked around by leaving the transmission in S rather than D, which holds gears longer at a cost to fuel economy.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: The advertised 33 mpg combined is achievable only in the driving mode the car is least pleasant in — a real-world gap between rated and delivered efficiency.
insights.locator: Even after days, this truculent response

insights.claim: Combined fuel economy is 33 mpg (29 city, 40 highway), better than similarly priced rivals like the Toyota Corolla or Kia K4, but only achievable by staying out of the turbo's power band.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: A direct competitive efficiency benchmark in the segment where fuel cost dominates total cost of ownership.
insights.locator: Fuel economy is a combined 33 mpg

insights.claim: The 2026 Jetta Sport requires a physical key inserted into a steering column lock to start, with no push-button start despite having remote locking.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Feature decontenting at the entry level has regressed to pre-2010 norms, showing where automakers cut to hold a $25k price against input-cost inflation.
insights.locator: For the 2026 standards, there are some novelties

insights.claim: The Jetta retains real physical buttons on its multifunction steering wheel because it never received the facelift that introduced VW's controversial capacitive wheel, though climate controls remain on a backlit capacitive panel.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Skipping a facelift accidentally preserved a feature customers preferred — evidence that VW's touch-control push was a net negative it is still unwinding.
insights.locator: The multifunction steering wheel also has real buttons

insights.claim: A persistent alert warned about winter tires every time the car exceeded 20 mph despite not being fitted with winter tires, and could only be disabled after consulting the manual.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Undiscoverable software nags are a recurring quality complaint that shows up in owner satisfaction scores long before mechanical issues do.
insights.locator: Learning how to modulate the throttle in heavy traffic

insights.claim: Using the transmission's manual mode to keep the engine out of the torque spike transformed the driving experience on twisty roads, reversing the author's initial verdict.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: The car's flaw is calibration, not capability — a software fix VW could ship, which is why the review reads as a missed opportunity rather than a bad product.
insights.quote: I expected to arrive at Cars and Coffee ready to mock the four-door VW, but I arrived a little humbled at how much I enjoyed the drive.
insights.locator: I thought I hated you, but I was wrong

insights.claim: The car uses its brakes as an electronic limited-slip differential, slowing a slipping wheel so torque routes to the side of the axle with grip, and the steering communicates enough front-tire information to judge cornering speed.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Brake-based torque vectoring delivers a mechanical-diff benefit at near-zero hardware cost — the standard software-substitutes-for-hardware play in cheap cars.
insights.locator: The steering gives you enough information
